evidence.snippet: Adult worms feed on the blood of a host and can cause iron deficiency anaemia

evidence.reference_title: Trichuris trichiura infection in children: Two case reports and literature review.
evidence.snippet: Most children with whipworm disease as well as blood in the stool present with mild to moderate small-cell hypochromic anemia, while severe anemia can be observed in certain cases.

nodes.description: Mucosal injury produces low-grade continuous bleeding into the gut lumen. Each adult worm accounts for roughly 0.005 mL of blood per day, so worm burden and duration of infection determine the cumulative loss.

evidence.reference_title: Trichuris trichiura infection in children: Two case reports and literature review.
evidence.snippet: the amount of bleeding caused by each adult parasite is 0.005 mL/d

evidence.reference_title: The public health significance of Trichuris trichiura.
evidence.snippet: The blood loss that can occur in T. trichiura infection is likely to contribute to anaemia

nodes.description: The embedded worm inflicts mechanical damage and chemical stimulation on the colonic mucosa. The degree of that mucosal injury tracks the clinical course of the infection.
nodes.id: Colonic mucosal mechanical and chemical injury

evidence.reference_title: Trichuris trichiura infection in children: Two case reports and literature review.
evidence.snippet: The clinical symptoms and course of the disease, the number of parasites and the response to treatment are closely related to the degree of intestinal mucosal injury.

nodes.description: Adult Trichuris trichiura burrow their slender anterior end into the epithelium of the cecum and colon, anchoring the worm in the mucosa. This is the initiating event of the whipworm arm, distinct from hookworm's direct blood-feeding mechanism.
nodes.id: Trichuris anterior-end embedding in colonic mucosa

evidence.reference_title: Trichuris trichiura infection in children: Two case reports and literature review.
evidence.snippet: The front end of the parasites burrows into the intestinal epithelium, feeds on blood and tissue fluid, and causes disease through mechanical damage, chemical stimulation and nutrient plundering in the host intestine.
